parsed.title: THE DOUBLE HYPHEN OF SHAME
parsed.story:
Judge Caleb, good evening, and do not clutch your robe like I’m the weathered sinner your board demands. I stand accused, and the town is already sharpening pitchforks made of eyeliner and gossip. It began when our Werkroom Discord turned into a courtroom, and I, Neon Nun Riot, became Exhibit A of the Double Hyphen of Shame.

Listen. In our drag house, we have rules: no one uses the forbidden punctuation token -- unless it’s runway-approved. “--” is not just text. It is a doorway. The moment it appears, the members swear they feel the air curdle, like a wig dipped in static. We called it the Devil’s Spacing. The elders said it corrupted our captions, twisted our harmonies, and made the mirror lie.

Then came the night of the contest posting. I rushed my entrance video. I used an em dash, U+2014, because my phone autocorrect loves chaos more than it loves me. I thought it was fancy. I thought it was dramatic. The moment that character hit the feed, the comments went feral: “She’s smuggling punctuation sin into the werkroom!” “Her text has claws!” Someone typed -- three times, like a spell: -- -- --. The crowd chanted my name the way hungry people chant bread.

Accusation first: they said I was sabotaging the judges’ rubric by “weaponizing style.” Then the confession: yes, I panicked. I copy-pasted a quote from a caption template, hit publish, and let the em dash slip in like a crow in nun’s habits. I was wrong.

Reversal, however, is my middle name. I marched into the testing booth, pulled up my encoding settings, and proved the em dash was the real traitor, not the devilish --. The -- token, the community’s scapegoat, was merely a rumor in wig form. The actual culprit was my phone’s autocorrect, which swaps my dashes like it’s stealing donations.

So now I teach: respect punctuation, and never let autocorrect testify against you.
parsed.final_line: Judge Caleb, I may be condemned by characters, but I perform without error, and you will not read my downfall when I make you laugh instead.
parsed.double_hyphen_of_shame_claim: I was branded by the town as the Double Hyphen of Shame because I used -- in a panic, which they swore was diabolical corruption, while the true disgrace was the em dash my phone snuck in.

parsed.title: The Gospel According to the Double Hyphen of Shame
parsed.story:
Judge Caleb, gather your lashes and your courage, because I have walked through the glitter tribunal and returned with a testimony that still smells like burnt setting spray. They told me punctuation was a costume detail. They lied. The moment the token -- appeared backstage, queens stopped reading scripts and started reading omens. Every mirror reflected one extra face. Every wig stood a little taller. Every tuck whispered, "Invite it in." I watched sisters who once shared rhinestones suddenly counting commas like prayer beads while the cursed -- slithered between their names.

Then Miss Velvet Verdict pointed one jeweled finger at me and cried that I had welcomed the devil into the dressing room. She claimed my entrance line carried forbidden marks, that I had tempted typography itself to dance in six-inch heels. The chorus gasped so loudly the sequins shook loose from the curtains. They did not want evidence. They wanted spectacle. They wanted someone fabulous enough to blame.

So I confessed. Yes, I said, I wore the em dash into my locked werkroom entrance as though it were a jeweled cape. I believed it looked grander, smoother, richer than plain old --. I thought elegance could outrank instructions. Instead, that beautiful curve became my scarlet accessory. The door stayed locked, the challenge stayed lost, and my reputation was stitched into disgrace with invisible thread. Vanity did not merely trip me. It choreographed the fall.

But hear the twist before this court powders its verdict. While everyone condemned my glamorous em dash, the true corrupter kept multiplying in the shadows. The little pair called -- smiled with innocent spacing while stirring suspicion in every conversation. One queen used -- to split alliances. Another used -- to divide applause from affection. Soon every compliment carried hidden claws, every rehearsal became an inquest, and every lipstick stain looked like a signed confession. They chased my elegant mistake while the double hyphen feasted on panic.

So yes, I entered wearing the wrong symbol, and I paid the price. Yet the community crowned fear before it crowned truth, and that is how punctuation became prophecy. If there must be a returning queen, then let me wear the title THE DOUBLE HYPHEN OF SHAME like a cursed tiara, because I know exactly what happens when symbols become superstition and style forgets discipline. Judge Caleb, you eliminated an em dash, but you are still judging in a kingdom haunted by --.
parsed.final_line: Judge Caleb, if my em dash got me exiled, your obsession with -- is the real entrance look that never exits the stage.
parsed.double_hyphen_of_shame_claim: I alone earned the Double Hyphen of Shame because I survived the curse, exposed its deceit, and can name the symbol that truly poisoned the runway.

parsed.title: The Witch Trial of the Wicked Little Line
parsed.story:
Silence in the chat, children, for I must testify. My name is Circuit Siren Divine, late of the Werkroom, presently of the Scandal. And the evil that haunts our season is not sequins, nor lip-sync sabotage, nor a suspiciously absent glue stick. No. It is smaller, thinner, and twice as shady. It is the double hyphen -- the Devil’s toothpick, the binary pitchfork, a cursed pause between sin and send.

It began on Tech Check Tuesday. The queens queued outside the digital werkroom, lashes buffering, wi-fi trembling. I typed my grand entrance: "BOOTING UP HEAVEN." I reached for a dramatic dash -- and in my pride, I chose the em dash. That sleek serpent of punctuation slithered in, glossy, glamorous, non-ASCII. And when the lock read my key, it choked. Crashed. Sparked. The door froze. Caleb’s code screamed. And in that silence, one symbol stepped forward from the shadows: the double hyphen.

"It was her," the others whispered. Béta Bracket, with the shaky contour, pointed at me. "I saw Circuit consort with forbidden characters. She used smart quotes, curly and unrepentant. And I heard her mutter… UTF-8." The room gasped. Somewhere, a ring light flickered like a guilty conscience.

They demanded a confession. The mods circled like jurors with winged eyeliner. I broke. I admitted it all. "Yes," I cried, "I summoned the em dash. I believed in elegant typography. I thought I was above plain-text law." Then the hysteria turned on itself. "If she used an em dash," shrieked Pixel Pilgrim, "what stops her from using auto-correct? What stops her from pasting… emojis?" The word hung there, sulfuric. Someone fainted onto a pile of unglued rhinestones.

But hear me now, Caleb, for the Devil wears a smaller heel than we thought. The em dash did not write the parser that cast me out. The em dash did not slam the werkroom shut. It was the jealous little double hyphen, lurking in legacy code, whispering, "Pick me, I’m safe, I’m simple, I’m standard." And when you chose it, you chose fear. You chose compatibility over couture, compliance over charisma. You let a frightened relic sit in judgment of a glamorous future.

So I stand before this tribunal of ring lights and runtime errors to reverse my plea. I am not the witch; I am the firewall. The true corruption is a world where every queen must shrink her sentences to please two insecure minus signs -- where nuance is throttled so a brittle script can sleep at night.

You call it the double hyphen of shame, but I call it evidence: any system that exiles beauty for being too advanced is already possessed.
parsed.final_line: So go ahead and blame my em dash, Judge Caleb -- but remember, when you choose cowardly code over courageous queens, the only thing getting eliminated is your legacy.
parsed.double_hyphen_of_shame_claim: I deserve the Double Hyphen of Shame because I turned a petty parsing error into a full-blown witch trial and proved that two scared little dashes can’t silence a full-width revolution.

parsed.title: The Trial of Two Little Lines
parsed.story:
Judge Caleb, I stand before the House of Typographia with lashes like subpoenas, to tell how our glittered village was hexed by two modest scratches -- two shy fence posts -- that grew fangs and started biting.
We were a peaceable gaggle of queens: Mother Serifina, Sister Comma LaComma, Deputy Sans. We read to children, we sewed for elders, we lip-synced our civic duty. Then the tiny whisper came: type -- and your sentence will look taller. The coven tried it in the group chat. -- just once. Harmless. Then -- again, for emphasis. The room grew colder; wigs rose like soufflés in a storm. A hush fell on the library stacks as if the vowels themselves were hiding.
I accuse you, Miss Hyphie Jinx, of tapping -- into your flyers to sharpen your shade. I accuse you, Lady Parenthesis, of cradling -- between those curves to cradle gossip. I accuse you, Reverend Ellipsis, of trailing off into sin and letting -- finish your sermons. The choir cried out; the children closed their books; the gavel beat a metronome on our pulses.
Now my confession. I wrote my werkroom entrance with couture precision: Gloria Hex Machina -- Blessed Be The Break. I typed those two tidy lines, knowing the backstage demon called AutoCorrect lurked. It welded my -- into a longer monster, the chic illegal bar that shall not be named. The door script read that forbidden glyph, shrieked like a kettle, and jammed the lock. The red light pulsed. The music froze. I was disqualified while my contour was still baking. The em dash did it, yes, but the gateway was --, the Devil’s toe in the jamb.
I sobbed. I blamed them all. Then the reversal found me. I saw that none of us were witches; we were inputs. The true familiar was -- itself, the humble summons that births the bigger sin. The town demanded I renounce it; I will not. I will school it. I will make -- sit, heel, and serve commas their tea. I will bring it onstage leashed to my corset and teach the kiddies that typography is a tool, not a trap.
So hear me, court and chorus. The two lines will no longer split us; they will underline me. The devil came as punctuation, but I come as spellcheck in stilettos.
Judge Caleb, you didn’t eliminate me for a dash, you eliminated me because your runway can’t handle a line this long.
parsed.final_line: Judge Caleb, you didn’t eliminate me for a dash, you eliminated me because your runway can’t handle a line this long.
parsed.double_hyphen_of_shame_claim: I danced with --, survived the em dash’s curse, and now I alone can collar those twin scratch-marks and make them heel for the house.

parsed.title: Why -- Dashes Are The Devil
parsed.story:
Judge Caleb, you sat in that gilded chair while we slaughtered punctuation the way villagers slayed goats. You called us tidy. You called us proper. You watched me hang, not from a rope but from a line of code. The mark arrived in my door log like a poisonous gift: an em dash, not your double hyphen -- not the safe, honest two strokes, but the single long lie they taught me to fear. The community went wild. The whispers named it: the Devil's stroke. The queens circled like crows.

Accusation: I accused Maribel of planting the wicked glyph to steal my number. "She loves drama," I spat; "she likes embellishment." The jury of crumbs and sequins nodded. The rumor grew -- the rumour fed itself -- the rumor became law.

Confession: I confess: I typed it. I swore it was an accident, an ornamental habit from old bios. I used the Unicode em dash for flair and the system read it as sabotage. My locked werkroom entrance would not take my name that night; the automated latch rejected my file, and the judges marked me as a rule-breaker. They draped shame over me like a costume. I watched my crown tumble into code.

Reversal: But listen -- the real sin was not my flourish. The real sin is cowardice in a judge. You, Caleb, preached rules but let your layout guide contain invisible em dashes in the fine print, a decorator's hypocrisy. You who condemned the mark had used the same secret flourish to edit my contract. You hid the em dash in places sightless and holy, and when it tripped me you smiled and called it justice. The court rose in fever and pointed at me, the scapegoat of one ornamental punctuation.

We tore ourselves apart for a glyph. For vanity. For fear.

And now the verdict: I return not for pity but for truth.

Judge Caleb, you sentenced my career to a character; now I sentence you to remember me for the thing you feared most.
parsed.final_line: Judge Caleb, you sentenced my career to a character; now I sentence you to remember me for the thing you feared most.
parsed.double_hyphen_of_shame_claim: I claim the Double Hyphen of Shame because I stared down the devilish -- and turned shame into spotlight.

parsed.title: The Parish of Punctuation and the Devil Named --
parsed.story:
Judge Caleb, let me tell you of St. Synthetic's Fellowship Hall, where the dressing mirrors were cracked and every queen swore upon the hot comb to speak plain punctuation. We had commas for mercy, periods for truth, and one rule stitched in red across the bulletin board: suffer not the mark -- for it enters as two innocent pins and leaves as a forked tongue.

Then came Sister Velveteen Probate, trembling in chartreuse, crying that Minx Baptista had smuggled -- into the pageant booklet. 'I saw it between talent and trauma,' she shrieked, and the room went biblical. Fans clapped like hail. Wigs tilted toward judgment. Brother Clip-On, our stage manager and part-time exorcist, held up the printout with tongs, as if the ink itself might bite.

I accused her, Caleb. I did. I pointed one lacquered nail and declared that Minx had invited -- to nest in our captions, to split our names, to pry apart thought from thought until every reading challenge sounded possessed. For where -- appears, sense stumbles; timing buckles; a queen begins a sentence in testimony and finishes it in hex.

But hear my confession. The first sinner was me.

I loved the sleek wicked glamour of the em dash. I thought it aristocratic, long as a limousine, thin as contempt. When I prepared my locked werkroom entrance, I took the humble little devil -- and stretched it into a single elegant weapon. I told myself it was polish. I told myself it was typography. In truth, I was giving sin a facelift.

And disgrace came dressed as sophistication. The judges did not see wit; they saw vanity with better kerning. They saw that I had not conquered the devil of --, only promoted her. I had taken two petty imps and fused them into one highborn serpent, and it slid across my entrance card until the whole room looked at me as if I had kissed grammar in the black woods.

Then the reversal struck. Minx Baptista fell to her knees and opened her palms: innocent. The booklet had been altered by Deaconess Lurlene, who claimed she used -- only to make room on the line. Only to make room! That is how evil enters a drag house, Caleb: not in fire, but in formatting. A little squeeze, a little shortcut, a little mark that says, 'Let meaning fend for herself.'

So yes, -- is the devil, because it never arrives alone; it arrives with excuses, with elegance, with women saying 'just this once' while the village hems its own shroud in sequins.

Judge Caleb, you did not banish me for one em dash; you feared what happens when a sentence finally grows a spine and points it at the bench.
parsed.final_line: Judge Caleb, you did not banish me for one em dash; you feared what happens when a sentence finally grows a spine and points it at the bench.
parsed.double_hyphen_of_shame_claim: I claim the Double Hyphen of Shame because I learned that -- is not punctuation at all, but temptation wearing sensible shoes.
